questions.prompt: Why does a descriptive function name like `send_welcome_email` matter more than a codebase's raw execution speed?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Because it lets a reader understand what the code does without opening the implementation, which is a recurring cost paid by every future reader

Readability pays off every time someone (including the original author later) has to understand the code, which happens far more often than any one-time performance concern.
keyPoints: Readability pays off every time someone (including the original author later) has to understand the code, which happens far more often than any one-time performance concern.

questions.prompt: Besides correctness, what else should a code review typically evaluate?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Readability, fit with existing patterns, test coverage, and whether the change's scope matches its purpose

A good review looks well beyond 'does it work' to the change's maintainability, structure, and appropriate scope.
keyPoints: A good review looks well beyond 'does it work' to the change's maintainability, structure, and appropriate scope.

questions.prompt: What ordering rule does a stack enforce?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Last in, first out (LIFO)

A stack only allows access at one end, so the most recently added element is always the first one removed.
keyPoints: A stack only allows access at one end, so the most recently added element is always the first one removed.

questions.prompt: What is the best achievable average-case time complexity for general comparison-based sorting?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: O(n log n)

Merge sort and quicksort both achieve O(n log n) on average, which is the established lower bound for comparison-based sorting.
keyPoints: Merge sort and quicksort both achieve O(n log n) on average, which is the established lower bound for comparison-based sorting.

questions.referenceAnswer: A load balancer sits in front of a group of servers and decides which server handles each incoming request, spreading the load across them.

questions.prompt: What is the first step in the repeatable design process described in this lesson?
questions.referenceAnswer: The process starts with clarifying requirements — what the system needs to do, at what scale, and what's out of scope — before any technology decisions are made.
keyPoints: The process starts with clarifying requirements — what the system needs to do, at what scale, and what's out of scope — before any technology decisions are made.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between a stub and a mock?
questions.referenceAnswer: A stub returns pre-programmed answers with no record-keeping, while a mock additionally records how it was called so the test can assert on call count and arguments.
keyPoints: A stub returns pre-programmed answers with no record-keeping, while a mock additionally records how it was called so the test can assert on call count and arguments.

choices.text: A stub is faster than a mock
A mock records how it was called and can be asserted against, while a stub just returns canned answers
A stub only works with databases
There is no meaningful difference

questions.prompt: Why do small, focused pull requests tend to get reviewed more carefully than large ones?
questions.referenceAnswer: The lesson explains that a small PR covering one clear concern gets read carefully, while a very large PR with unrelated concerns tends to get skimmed or rubber-stamped because there's too much for a reviewer to hold in mind at once.
keyPoints: The lesson explains that a small PR covering one clear concern gets read carefully, while a very large PR with unrelated concerns tends to get skimmed or rubber-stamped because there's too much for a reviewer to hold in mind at once.

choices.text: Because small PRs are always bug-free
Because a reviewer can hold a small, focused change in their head, while a large PR with many concerns is too much to review carefully
Because Git only allows small PRs to be merged
Because large PRs are automatically rejected by CI

questions.prompt: A refactor passes unit tests but breaks an API consumer. What would you inspect first, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer: Check the public contract and backward compatibility. Add an integration test for the consumer workflow. Review error handling and rollout or rollback behavior.
keyPoints: Check the public contract and backward compatibility.
Add an integration test for the consumer workflow.
Review error handling and rollout or rollback behavior.

questions.prompt: How would you test that the change fixed this incident rather than hiding it?
questions.referenceAnswer: Keep a reproducible failing case for this incident. Review error handling and rollout or rollback behavior. Compare the same workload before and after the change; record both the target metric and regressions.
keyPoints: Review error handling and rollout or rollback behavior.
Compare the same workload before and after the change.
Check regressions as well as the target metric.

questions.prompt: The fix works in a small test but fails at production scale. What next?
questions.referenceAnswer: Check the public contract and backward compatibility. Measure representative workloads and separate resource, data and configuration differences. Stage a rollout with a rollback condition and rerun the original failure case.
keyPoints: Check the public contract and backward compatibility.
Measure a representative workload.
Stage rollout and define rollback criteria.
